text:
As the economy of the world seeks more solid footing in 2009, some distortions to clean petroleum product trade routes seem not only likely but even inevitable. Although near-term demand for clean products remains unclear, delays to projects being considered by the refining industry are the real drivers in the shipping market.
Just a year ago, export-oriented refineries seemed to show a clear future of clean product trade development. Now, however, it is on the shoulders of the tanker market to fill any gaps in spot demand. Complicated product specifications and regulations not only keep trade patterns shifting and erratic but also create arbitrage opportunities aplenty, especially when cold weather occurs in one region or when some other disruption hits the logistical supply chain.
Clean product tanker trading is really a demand driven market. With Americans seeming to have given up on their appetite for smaller cars now that the price of gasoline has fallen in half, enough demand should materialize to keep this fleet actively engaged for 2009.

As the Obama Administration continues to rev its policy engines, sacred cows of many self-interest groups may become road-kill on the United States' bio-fueled road towards energy independence. For instance, by the Administration's willingness to reconsider whether states should set auto emission limits stricter than the Environmental Protection Agency's, the bedraggled US automotive industry is now being haunted by the de facto spectre of producing cars with greater fuel efficiency. In the fuel camp, word from the EPA on how to incorporate a lifecycle analysis of the carbon footprint of fuels used to meet the Renewable Fuel Standard, is awaited anxiously. The decision was deferred by the Bush Administration. Resolution by the Obama Administration will signal where it stands in the evolving international debate surrounding bio-fuel sustainability. By using an objective criterion such as lifecycle analysis to assess overall economic and environmental impact of fuel, the air might quickly be cleared of any marketing claims of renewability that are even remotely misleading.
While expanding use of home-grown fuels was a theme during 2008's Presidential election campaign, their presence grows sharply through 2020 under the current renewable fuels standard even without a new mandate to push additional bio-fuel volumes into gasoline.

Given indications made on last year's campaign trail, one can envisage a landscape where US gasoline is forced to ingest quantities of ethanol even greater than those presently mandated. With the contraction of the global economy, the question on the minds of many is how it will affect the tanker market in the immediate term. Although tankers is still one of the most viable shipping sectors, the last few months have seen asset prices soften, newbuilding orders cease and freight rates return to long-term averages. In attempts to answer the question, we turn our attention to the physical crude tanker market to see what happened so far this year.
The graph below is a reflection of the past four months (October through January) of dirty fixture activity year-on-year for 2007-2008 and 2008-2009. Across the major dirty trading sectors, spot activity has decreased on a number of trades. Potential factors include the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and Non-OPEC production cuts and more importantly decreased demand in the OECD countries. The VLCC sector was most noticeably affected showing a 13% decrease in volume in the comparable periods.

As the winds of misfortune shape the revival of the World's economic future, a maxim - perhaps forgotten by some - still rings ever true. In real estate ventures, the accepted recipe for success is "location, location, location" and nowadays some players in the shipping industry see this recipe as "relationship, relationship, relationship." At the 15th annual Joint Shipping Conference held in New York City this week, the importance of established relationships emerged as a central theme. Ship owners, bankers, and other industry professionals were gathered there to ponder the question of "How Will Shipping Survive the Perfect Storm?"
With a seemingly pervasive sentiment, attendees viewed the current "storm" pattern as different from prior downturns weathered by the shipping industry. Additionally, common to both bankers and ship owners was their focus on the importance of relationships in structuring deals. According to conference panelists, banks are currently deleveraging and these measures have significantly impeded the availability of ship financing. This constriction may continue for, perhaps, another 18 months. During their flight to quality, banks seem to prefer customers with whom they have established relationships. But even their established customers have witnessed substantial adjustments in traditional banking relationships. While the shape of vessel financing may be undergoing a nip and tuck facelift, established and strong relationships - as always - remain a pivotal key to launching deals.
Some participants wondered if the shipping industry was entering a period reminiscent of one characteristic of a decade ago. Back then, the sale and purchase of assets provided a ready source of revenue to some owners. This breed of owner placed value on acquiring vessel assets at seemingly bargain prices with the intention of subsequently selling them at better prices. Sometimes a low acquired priced vessel might be retained - even though its owner saw a higher resale price - if the expectations for the asset's future time charter rates were strong. Should the tacit of buying low in the hope of selling higher become more widely adopted, opportunities for attracting private capital may reappear. Additionally, even those owners who are focused on the financial power of extended time charters to carry their vessels - and perhaps less on the relative price of the asset - may now also look specifically to acquire valued assets with prices deemed to be low.
Some ship owners are in a mode to just survive this economic downturn. Other players - perhaps with deeper pockets - seem poised, however, to not only survive, but more importantly, to resume their drive to thrive as these uncertain times abate.

This week the global market continued to feel the weight of the 800 pound gorilla pressing down, dashing any hopes of a near-term economic recovery. The impending implementation of the ILO Maritime Convention 2006 will bring more stringent regulations intending to improve the life of the seafarer. On a practical basis this convention will have very real implications on ship operations and commercial activity.
In a nutshell, the ILO has consolidated over 68 existing instruments involving health standards, working and living conditions, welfare and medical care issues and recruitment and retention issues to name a few. Shipowners, shipboard officers and the supporting cast of the maritime industry will be expected to follow the changes brought forth through the titles below: Title I: Minimum requirements for seafarers to work on a ship Title II: Conditions of Employment Title III: Accommodation, recreational facilities, food and catering Title IV: Health protection, medical care, welfare and soc. sec. protection Title V: Compliance and enforcement The Maritime Labor Convention 2006 has already been adopted by five major flag states (Norway, Liberia, Marshall Islands, Bahamas and Panama) and several ILO members. Originally conceived in February 2006 at a maritime session in Geneva, Switzerland, the ILO Convention grew into what is now being called the "fourth pillar" of the IMO's regulatory regime for shipping along with the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, 1974 (SOLAS), the International Convention on Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping, 1978 (STCW), and the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships, 1973/78 (MARPOL). The aggressive five‐year ILO action plan is to have the Convention ratified in 2011 and implemented by 2012. As shown in the chart below, the tanker fleet has significant representation of the leading flag states to ratify the convention.

Although the Convention has good intentions, opening the door to a better lifestyle at sea, the underlying implications will undoubtedly squeeze shipowners. Often, shipowners can pass transparent costs, such as bunkers, along to charterers through changes in the annual flat rate, though operating expenses are a trickier story. It is unlikely charterers will have much sympathy for shipowners on less tangible expenses such as quality of life for the crew.
Perhaps, the most striking outcome is the disruption of world commerce that could arise through increased ship detentions. In the European Union alone, the ILO reported that the number of ship detentions is on the rise from 944 in 2005 to 1,250 in 2007, an increase of 32% over just two years justifying a need for increased standard port inspections. Estimating the holdings of unseen petroleum reservoirs - especially those located deep beneath the seabed - is a daunting and imprecise task. Although estimates of established fields usually benefit from seismic and other geological information accumulated over time, estimates of reserves in new discoveries usually lack this luxury.
Media rumblings of significant new crude oil finds are typically reported as best estimates based on preliminary data. These guesses are, of course, subject to later tweaking and revision. With this caveat in mind, the gathering of guesses surrounding the reserve potential of oil in offshore Cuban fields - on face value - seems destined to give this island nation a great leap forward into the club of net oil exporters.

Cuba's estimate of offshore oil reserves amounts to nearly the quantity of the United States proven crude oil reserves in 2007. If the US produced some 4.6 million barrels per day of crude oil from its reserves of 21.3 billion barrels, how much oil would Cuba likely produce per day? Assuming a similar pumping to reserve ratio as the US uses, Cuba would be able to produce oil for a little over 12 years - just like the US.
One "what if" is presently not a politically feasible option. While the US would be a refinery‐ready market for Cuba's oil, current legislation makes US refineries neither willing nor able to process it. So with a logical market forbidden, where will Cuban oil go? If the properties of their new offshore reserves mirrors that of Cuba's typical heavy (below 20 degree API gravity) crude oil, any production left over from domestic use may have to travel far to find a home capable of upgrading it. Although it seems premature to even speculate on how much oil will move and where it might move to, tanker owners might take some comfort in the view that a new source of oil production needing transportation to distant markets might eventually appear.
However, what if the US does - for whatever reason - become an outlet for Cuban oil? With the steady decline in its own production, any influx of nearby Cuban oil would mute the hopes of tankers owners expecting an expansion of longer‐haul routes for replacement oil into the US.
How close reality comes to present estimates of Cuban oil reserves will play a role in its eventual production rate. The cost and ease of production as well as the crude oil's properties will also be reflected in this rate. So for now, tanker owners might consider bookmarking Cuba's oil discovery. The twist and turns in this unfolding story of the further exploration and development work to wrest oil from these deep offshore fields may yet impact tanker markets.

In 2006, the Panama Canal Authority (ACP) announced a $5.25 billion expansion proposal. It was a period of global economic growth and expanding shipping markets. Now, just three years later, the project finds itself in a very different environment. The expansion plans to create a third canal capable of handling post‐Panamax container vessels, up to 366 meters in length with a 49 meter beam, and a draft that would allow Capesize bulkers and Suezmax passages. The shipping shortcut joining the two largest oceans is destined for expansion by 2014; the question now is whether or not customers will be looking to take advantage.
The Panama Canal opened and closed its locks to over 14,000 ships in 2008, carrying over 200 million tons of cargo and yielding a toll revenue of over $1.3 billion. According to the ACP, tanker traffic accounted for 1,916 of the transits or roughly 13% of the total.
The chart below provides an overview of the toll revenues over the past three fiscal years (October to September). The upward growth trend helps justify the expansion. Even in crumbling economic conditions, the Canal saw an increase in transits of 0.1% in the first quarter of fiscal year 2009 (fourth quarter of calendar year 2008).

The tanker fleet is faced with a very large orderbook. The reason the market is in such a position today can be explained by a theory applied to population growth known as The Tragedy of the Commons . Under this premise, individuals will behave rationally, acting in their own best interest to maximize individual gains. However, in doing so, the individual ultimately destroys the underlying common resource and thus the very source of their gains.
The example is illustrated by a collection of herders that share a common grazing area. Each herder is incentivized to add to their herd, benefiting individually from the earnings of each additional animal. Yet the common grazing area is finite and can only support a finite number of animals. Thus, the commons will become overgrazed and each herder will end up in a worse position than if they had behaved with a collective responsibility. The challenge for the individual then becomes deciding whether to maximize individual gains at the expense of the commons or to prolong individual gains by protecting the commons. Despite the logic in preserving the commons, few herders are likely to stand on the sidelines as others share in the spoils. In a time of record earnings and vessel prices many shipowners and shipyards demonstrated herder mentalities by grazing in the same market.
This illustration is particularly relevant in light of overbuilding taking place in the shipping markets. The chart below shows the orderbook for tankers by type and percent on order versus the existing fleet.

While supply and demand fundamentals along with price arbitrage will determine its basic direction, the international transportation fuels market will confront an increasingly complex environment in the years to come. In attempting to project that future environment, technology and policy are the biggest unknowns.
An evolution of environmental and tax policy as well as technology are necessary before biofuels can significantly impact transportation fuels consumption; biofuels accounted for just one percent of total road transportation fuel supply in 2008. It is now clear that while policies have succeeded in ensuring that biofuels will play a role in the future transportation fuels mix, a host of economic, infrastructural and political constraints also suggest that their role is not likely to be fully defined for years to come. Focus has sharpened on the development of "second‐generation" non‐grain feedstocks that should assuage food security concerns, but experts say this new generation is 10 to 15 years from wide‐scale adoption with many hurdles to yet overcome.
The expanding use of electronic and hybrid vehicles is unlikely to moderate transportation fuels demand within the medium term. Billions in research funding at home and abroad is bound to produce significant technological breakthroughs, but rapid mass‐scale adoption of these new technologies would take years even under typical fleet replacement trends. The challenges facing new vehicle technologies were made evident recently when the Energy Department announced an end to its research into hydrogen fuel‐cells, a technology previously hailed as key to a carbon‐neutral economy, because they will not be commercially practical over the next 10 to 20 years.
The economic crisis has inspired a lively international debate about the appropriate role of government at a time when many nations, including the United States, face challenges only governments have the resources to address. The blurring line between public and private interests will have tangible impacts on the energy industry as governments adjust policies such as price controls and subsidies that directly impact supply and demand and stringent environmental regulations that pose significant challenges to industry.

text: Test #1 Test #2 Test #3 The most logical starting point for performing the analysis is the historical Worldscale rates themselves. But since Worldscale rates do not exist in a vacuum other factors were considered. After combing through 30 potential factors, the following had the strongest correlations: a) VLCC one‐year timecharter rates b) VLCC three‐year timecharter rates c) VLCC Scrap Value d) Spot vessel availability e) US crude oil stocks f) Crude oil price per barrel g) OPEC production level h) Bunker prices Putting it to the Test Although it is clear that Worldscale depends on different factors, the first method (autoregressive vector) sourced only historical Worldscale rates to generate an outlook. The analysis used 200 data points and the series provided very little correlation to the actual Worldscale data. The next test consisted of several rounds of multiple regressions with statistical software to consider the eight variables as external influences. The variables that were initially found to be the most influential on the Worldscale rates were the last month's Worldscale rate, the number of ships available in the AG for the next month and the VLCC 1‐year time charter rates. Upon further drilling into the conditionality of these variables, it was concluded that the 1‐year time charter rates were not statistically significant in formulating a short‐term outlook. In the final analysis, all eight variables were considered to be endogenous, acting upon each other as a system. When approached in this method, the variables produced a more closely correlated result to the actual rate progression. The one variable, however, that seemed to stand out as one of the most statistically significant was the spot availability of ships over the next 30 days. Perhaps less by choice and more because of a call by media and lawmakers, Chu has gone from a Nobel Prize winning physicist, to a man with the power to shape and mold the future of US energy policy and arguably the world. Awash with new policy ideas, Secretary Chu finds himself in between an alternative energy horizon and reliable, efficient oil. In addition to linking the price of oil to economic recovery, Chu safely believes that the price is the result of market psychology and the prospect for future supply and demand. Crude oil has never proven to be a dull commodity especially for those entangled in its web of commerce. Be it the volatile environment in which to buy and sell it or move it, or perhaps even its glamour as being the 'black gold,' its fluctuation sometimes takes the market for a wild ride. In the past six months, it's danced the contango, offering traders and charterers of ships the chance to scoop up the liquid commodity at a low spot price and make cash from higher future prices. In tankers, this has led to the waterborne storage of roughly 80‐90 million barrels of oil primarily aboard VLCCs. However, as the spot price of oil continues to rise, this contango opportunity may be fading fast.
Earlier this week, even at the price of $70 per barrel, West Texas Intermediate (WTI) was trading futures at higher levels, giving incentive to fix ships for storage. But by the end of this same week, oil broached $72 per barrel and futures did not follow upward. So the contango structure seems snuffed for now. But it could be argued that this is just a brief pause for the unique market play. However, even if this is the case, how many times can the contango fade in and out and how much oil can truly be stockpiled worldwide? Market fundamentals would suggest that this uptick in spot crude prices is a reflection of illogical market psychology rather than being rooted in current supply and demand fundamentals.

The slight rally in the crude tanker freight rates has left many wondering if the crude tanker market is actually resilient enough to emerge from the financial crisis relatively unscathed. Over the past two weeks the market has gained momentum, with the VLCCs out of the Arabian Gulf bound for the Far East breaching $40,000 per day, spurring increased bullishness on the part of shipowners and oil companies. Only last month nearly all sectors of the market were bottom feeding, earning charter rates sufficiently below break‐even levels.
Although it is tough to say that a recovery is imminent, the sentiment has certainly improved ‐ even if only temporarily. The challenge now becomes navigating a rate environment that still seems to carry an element of surprise. While there is a tendency to paint all shipping sectors with one brush, it is important to remember a few key characteristics in the tanker market. Trade demand is essentially driven by fundamental economic strength. While other shipping sectors are dependent on slightly more fickle drivers such as discretionary consumer spending or construction demand, energy remains a necessity for survival.
Slight positive movements in a broader economic recovery will yield immediate results in the physical oil markets. For example, the number of Arabian Gulf spot market VLCC liftings has seen a very slight increase month‐on‐month. Additionally, the highly liquid and fairly consolidated spot market complicates and obscures the available tanker supply. As we have been painfully aware for several months, piracy off the coast of Somalia has been on the rise since 2007 and it poses an increasing effect to the shipping industry. With the Somalian government too shaky to take effective measures, the onus has fallen upon other governments and the shipping industry itself. But questions remain: how is piracy to be combated? Who will shoulder the costs? And how will the market reorient itself around this escalation of crime?
Neither piracy nor its presence in the Gulf of Aden is new, but the main cause for alarm about the situation in Somalia is the exponential growth: there were two attempted attacks in 2004, but 42 in 2007. And while the Somalian government is located in the capital, Mogadishu, the vast majority of the pirates are based in the breakaway region of Puntland. As a result, the Somalian government lacks the resources and the influence to mount a campaign against the pirates, or solve the socioeconomic problems that make piracy so appealing.

Clearly, the situation calls for government intervention, and fast: the Somalian government has issued a plea for funds to create its own coast guard, and the United States already spear‐heads the Combined Task Force 151 (CTF‐151). The CTF‐151 includes vessels from the United Kingdom, Australia, France, Germany, Italy, Pakistan and Japan as well as aircrafts that aid in patrolling the Gulf of Aden. But this large naval presence has only moderately inhibited the pirates. Now what?
The first option is to organize shipping into a safe lane; the existence of a heavily secured lane would make it easier for international forces in the area to monitor shipping and respond to distress calls. However, if the naval forces fail to provide complete security, the lane has the effect of herding all the potential targets together in an accessible location. The second is to provide a coastguard for Somalia; but in the absence of a long‐term and reliable government to either maintain a coastguard or prosecute pirates, the existence of a weak coastguard would only result in free training for future pirates and further loss of money. The final option is to stop paying ransoms, a solution suggested by those who argue that a lack of incentive is key to safer seas for all concerned. However, the Somalian pirates might adopt the practices of their Indonesian colleagues and create phantom ships (a stolen ship that is re‐registered and then has its cargo 'stolen') or switch to stealing cargo. Each option would result in a tactical shift for the pirates-something that the shipping industry is reluctant to induce, in the event that it creates a more sophisticated breed of Somalian pirate.
As unwelcome as the news is, the solution lies in fixing Somalia's political situation; only with a stable government in place can the pirates be ousted from their haven. Until then, the presence of warships cannot suffice for the expenses incurred from ship re‐ routing. An industry‐wide refusal to pay ransom would be difficult to implement- especially when human life is involved. The alpha and omega of this situation is Somalia's internal stability: and only when this is addressed can this glut of piracy end.

After duking it out with the economy in the second half of 2008, the tanker and dry bulk market took a hard fought 12 th round tumble. Rumors have circulated that 20‐60% of the global orderbook may be cancelled or delayed. Shipyards have scrambled to enforce contracts with their clients and generate some semblance of a cash flow. On top of this uncertainty, outlooks from the International Energy Agency (IEA) seem continually revised to reflect falling global oil demand. This plight shared by the involved yards and owners is only going to get more painful.
Since the third quarter of 2008, this sentiment has been increasingly pervasive in articles and press releases-but it may be fundamentally flawed. The worldwide recession has undoubtedly affected the tanker and dry bulk markets, but it has not unleashed a demon. Instead, it has checked the exuberance of a market which contains a 50% unfinanced orderbook and yards that suffer from 15% to 35% orderbook slippage. New tanker supply has been curtailed in the wake of delays and the phase‐out of single hulls has slowed for tankers in low rate environments.
As can be seen below, the tanker orderbook is experiencing an imbalance in the ratio of deliveries to vessels left on order for this year. While uncovering the extent of these delays will not be known until the year is through, the carry over of fourth quarter 2008 deliveries into the beginning of this year hints at what may lie on the horizon.

The $250 billion shortfall within a $500 billion orderbook resembles the VLCC ordering frenzy that took pace in the mid 1970's: in both cases, the number of unfinanced newbuildings presented a substantial problem. Currently, banks lack the capacity to fix this gap and with more rigorous credit requirements since the downturn began, they are reluctant to throw money at anyone, let alone in the shipping industry. This lack of financing appears grim, but it is useful in exposing the flimsy nature of the newbuilding orderbook.
For example, if a newbuilding contract never receives the final stamp of approval or adequate funding in the first place then its legitimacy as taking part in the orderbook is tentative at best. By removing these 'newbuildings' from an analysis of cancelled orders, the outlook no longer curdles the blood. The tanker orderbook would see approximately a 5% decrease and the dry bulk market-arguably the hardest hit sector-would lose roughly 10‐15% of its orderbook.
Throughout this ordering glut and global recession, both yards and owners have tried to maintain their delicate relationship, making cancelling a difficult endeavor. One notable exception to this is Frontline, who cancelled two VLCCs and four Suezmaxes; a move that reduced their orderbook by about a third, equivalent to $556 million. However, larger owners like Frontline, are generally granted more wiggle room than owners with only a few ships on order-and it is these owners who make up the majority of the orderbook.
In fact, the yards possess a remarkable amount of clout; despite being plagued by orderbook backlog, they have been highly resistant to price cuts or additional delays demanded by owners. The financial weight of the new IMO standards, which will be required in all vessels delivered after January 1, 2012, will include more efficient engines, water‐treatment systems and ballast tank coating. The new standards of coating alone are predicted to add roughly a 2% increase to newbuilding costs. The yards appear to be protecting their orderbooks from cancellations-a situation at odds with the reality that most tankers face a delay of 6 months or more.
A solution to this puzzle is government backing: by stimulating the yards and seeking to prevent ship abandonment, incentives are provided to both owners and yards to maintain a stable and constant relationship.

Nestled between the two largest proven reserves of oil, Saudi Arabia and Iran, Iraq follows suit as the third largest proven conventional oil‐reserve at approximately 115 billion bbls. Unlike many of its Middle‐Eastern counterparts, the past five years have created a difficult environment to compete in the commercial oil trade, however this is about to change. Faced with surging fuel prices at a time of weak earnings and depressed demand, owners currently mired in the summer doldrums find themselves asking: what's causing the rise in bunker prices and how long can it be sustained? This time it is not just the universal increase in crude oil price that is causing bunker prices to rise.
Sometimes, the effect of similar bunker price hikes has been muted by higher earnings. The narrowing differential between light and heavy crude oils is playing a leading role in the recent rise in the cost of bunker fuel. As sources of heavy crude oil production hold back for whatever reason, refineries configured to process these traditionally less‐ expensive heavy oils have been forced to pay higher prices. In January, 3% sulfur fuel oil in the US Gulf Coast was assessed above New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) light sweet crude oil for the first time since 1986. Any lightening of the world's crude oil slate in coming years, suggested by the lack of significant new discoveries of heavy crude oil, mean this dynamic could continue pushing up prices.
The change in the light/heavy price differential is being compounded by the addition of upgrading capacity at refineries around the world. Upgrading margins, the profit refiners draw from processing heavy crude oils into more valuable products like gasoline and diesel, have collapsed recently and are likely to come under even more pressure as projects slowed by the economic crisis finally come on‐stream. The IEA predicts 6.5 mb/d of upgrading capacity will be added by 2014 and the Paris‐based agency expects these additions will contribute to a "substantial tightening" of fuel oil markets in coming years.

As of the end of July, fuel costs were 60 % of voyage revenue for a VLCC on the benchmark Arabian Gulf ‐ Far East voyage. Last week, 500,000 bbls of Colombian Castilla blend crude oil flowed through the Petroterminal de Panama (PTP) pipeline in Panama. The cargo was the pipeline's first to flow from east to west and the reversal in flow direction mirrors a shift in petroleum trading patterns from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Although questions remain about the reversal's ultimate impact on international trade flows, the reversed PTP pipeline may come to have significant implications for and the tanker market.
Owned jointly by the Government of Panama, Castor Petroleum, and Northvillle Industries, (operator of the port) PTP is an 81‐mile pipeline connecting Chiriqui Grande on Atlantic Coast to Charco Azul on the Pacific. The pipeline was built in 1982 to transport Alaskan crude oil to markets to the east and at its peak moved 800 kbd. More than 3.5 billion bbls moved through the pipeline between 1982 and 1996, when the pipeline was closed as volumes of Alaskan crude oil began to dwindle. The recent reversal of the PTP's flow is expected to have only a marginal impact on ton‐mile demand as it is focused mainly on the movements of tankers loading in the Caribbean bound to the West Coast of the US and maybe even the Far East.
The US West Coast was once rich with crude oil from Alaska and California, but in recent years has seen the growing presence of imports from foreign sources, a trend set to continue in the future. As shown in the chart below, crude oil imported to the US West Coast from the Arabian Gulf has grown almost ten percent over the past 15 years.

The pipeline is primarily expected to help provide refiners on the US West Coast with a wider variety of crude oils. Tesoro signed a seven‐year agreement last December to ship 107 kbd through the reversed pipeline in order to supply its five largest refineries, located in California, Washington, Hawaii and Alaska. BP has a seven‐year contract to ship 65 kbd through the PTP pipeline and expects the reversal to cut transit times for Angolan crude oil to the US West Coast by seven days. The reversed pipeline is also expected to ease the transportation times of crude oils from the North Sea, Columbia and other Atlantic Basin sources of crude oil.
The map below relates two methods of transporting crude oil out of the Arabian Gulf to the US West Coast refineries.
Traditionally, VLCCs steam east out of the Arabian Gulf when bound for the US West Coast, with an average voyage length of 37 days. While the alternative of using the PTP pipeline presents 47‐ day voyages, the prospect of an owner securing a backhaul cargo out of the Caribbean would provide enticing freight economics. In this market, however, a lack of cargoes and a surplus of vessel availabilities will likely deter owners from having great success with this alternative.
The PTP will now act as a competitor to the Panama Canal, one of the world's shipping choke points, for crude oil movements; however, there are additional costs to be considered before jumping into the waiting line for the 81‐mile expanse of Panama. The savings on tanker freight earned by pushing barrels through the PTP are yet to be seen, especially in the current freight rate environment. To really determine whether the PTP offers any savings, charterers will be forced to consider the risks of terminal delays, storage costs and pipeline transit charges.
The PTP pipeline reversal is another demonstration of the way evolving trade patterns are changing the infrastructure developed to service worldwide petroleum demand a generation ago. While depressed rates blunt the immediate impact the pipeline's reversal could have on the tanker market, as freight rates start to recover, the pipeline may become a more attractive option in the long‐term.
When demand recovers, the PTP pipeline will prove to be a valuable conduit for crude oil going to West Coast refineries, but do not expect this to have a significant impact on worldwide ton‐ mile demand.

Much of this region's new oil demand probably never saw the inside of a tanker for very long as it was consumed near where it was produced. From 2009 to 2010, the IEA's outlook is that China's and the Middle East's oil demand each will lift by 0.3 mbd.
While some practitioners of the dismal science - more commonly referred to as economists - see the buds of a recovery, caution is still wise in acting on their view. Assessing tanker demand in the cloudy, shifting times surrounding any economic recovery seems bound to yield erratic indications. Careful pinpointing of emerging and perhaps even fading trade routes is essential to understanding how the recovery of ton‐mile demand will progress. Some oil demand stalwarts of last cycle's economic expansion may not have quite the same vigor in the next one, while others might easily show as much or even more demand as in the past. Agile tanker market participants should position themselves to seize asset opportunities when and where they appear to mesh with expectations of ton‐miles demand recovery.

At the moment, the specter of tightening regulation is a fact of life across nearly every niche of the energy industry. Governments worldwide are working both separately and together to develop limits on sulfur and carbon emissions from industry, improvements in mileage standards for automobiles and better oversight of derivatives trading. While all of these regulatory efforts will eventually impact the tanker industry, the effort to reduce sulfur content of marine bunker fuels is of immediate concern for both the bunkering and shipping industries.
The International Maritime Organization (IMO) adopted regulations last October calling for the sulfur content of marine bunker fuel within existing Emissions Control Areas (ECAs) to drop from existing limits of 1.5%S to 0.1%S by 2015. The group also approved a decrease in the maximum permissible sulfur content outside of the designated areas from the 4.5%S today to 3.5%S in 2012, and proposed a 0.5%S cap by 2020.
Particularly significant for US shipowners will be the introduction of a North American ECA as early as August 2012, the area of which is related in the map below.
The proposed area of the ECA includes U.S. and Canadian waters adjacent to the Pacific coast, the Atlantic/Gulf coast and the eight main Hawaiian Islands. The proposed ECA would extend 200 nautical miles from the coastal baseline. France has joined the ECA proposal on behalf of its island territories off the coast of Newfoundland. Mexico is also considering joining the N.A. ECA initiative.

IMO regulations limiting the fuel sulfur content burned within Emission Control Areas (ECAs) were announced earlier this decade. Demand for low sulfur heavy residual bunkers is rendered inelastic at a given level of traffic by the ECAs' mandates. On the supply side, how much of these bunkers come from local refineries and how much come from areas outside the ECAs ultimately depends on its price. There is no magic way for local refineries to either easily or cheaply reduce bunker sulfur content. Refineries in neighboring regions seem a likely source from where any shortfall of 1% sulfur bunker fuel will be pulled. Finding enough stocks to blend, however, will certainly be more daunting than blending the current sulfur requirement. A restrictive limit on the concentrations of aluminum plus silicon will also crimp refiners' blending options.
The bunker fuel sulfur limit in the ECAs will be further reduced from 1.0%S to 0.1%S starting January 1, 2015. Vessels operating in the designated areas of northwest Europe and North America must burn compliant marine fuel oil subject to the IMO "fuel availability" provision. This step‐function change in fuel quality will require vessels to consume marine distillates in place of low sulfur residual fuel oil. This further tightening of marine fuel sulfur requirements will impact distillate balances in both North America and Europe and test refiners' ability to meet this incremental demand. Regional pricing arbitrages and trade routes will no doubt be impacted.
On a global basis, the change from maximum 4.5%S content and 3.5%S effective January 1, 2012, should not present any insurmountable problems for the Industry since the current average sulfur level supplied is approximately 2.7%S as measured by current IMO methodology.
Longer term, however, the drastic reduction in the marine fuels sulfur cap from 3.5%S to 0.5%S in 2020 (subject to an IMO feasibility study in 2018), will present significant challenges for the Industry. Given current technology, refiners do not have the capability to produce residual fuel oil at this level of sulfur; neither does the refining industry have the economic incentive to add this type of capability.

Prior to the Hebei Spirit incident in December 2007, South Korea was generally expected to allow non‐double hull tankers to trade in its ports through 2015. South Korea had long been the top discharge port for the single hull tankers that were the subject of International Maritime Organization (IMO) regulations requiring the vessels stop trading by 2015. The accident spilled 75,000 barrels of crude oil into the Yellow Sea, caused more than $500 million in damage and inspired South Korea to accelerate the ban on single hull ships to 2010. The United Arab Emirates followed suit by announcing that it too would prohibit the use of single hull tankers from 2010.
Other countries have also voiced concerns about single hull ships trading within their waters and have intimated regulations could be on the horizon, however this remains to be seen.
At present, IMO regulations ban single hull tankers from trading after 2010 or when they reach 25 years of age, but allow them to continue until 2015 with permission from port states and approval under the Conditional Assessment Scheme.

At the onset of the financial crisis last year, the fourth quarter of 2009 was targeted as the likely beginning of a recovery in the international economy. With the fourth quarter now upon us, things are, in fact, undeniably less bad than they have been. There are budding signs of life in the international economy. Can tanker freight‐rates be far behind? Despite some lingering uncertainty about the future, there is a sense that the tanker market may have already seen the worst.
In its Oil Market Report released last month, the International Energy Agency (IEA) indicated it expected worldwide demand to lift by 300 kb/d in the fourth quarter of 2009 ‐ the first such demand growth in the last five quarters. That marginal increase in demand could herald the early stages of economic recovery.
Improvements in both Chinese and US economic data were cited as the main drivers for the upward revision of the IEA's August projection of 2009 demand. Much has been made of the role that China has played in shifting the focus of petroleum and ton‐mile demand growth outside of the OECD. However, the OECD is now expected be the focal point of demand recovery in the fourth quarter. As shown in the table below, OECD demand is expected to increase by 900 kb/d in the fourth quarter of 2009 while non‐OECD demand contracts by 600 kb/d.

While supply and demand fundamentals dictate that the long‐term focus of demand growth will return to the non‐OECD countries, the short‐term improvements in OECD demand present a reason for some hope amid the discouragement that has prevailed for months.
Beyond lagging oil demand, the tanker market faces other challenges. The storage of crude oil and petroleum products at sea has been an important factor in the tanker market throughout 2009. It can be argued that the use of tankers as floating storage by refiners, oil majors, and traders has helped support freight rates by providing term employment for ships in a challenging rate environment. The contango structure in crude oil markets which inspired the uptick in storage fixtures has narrowed since the first quarter of this year and there are indications that the dynamics of floating storage are in flux. Some players who have been storing crude oil on tankers appear to have changed their strategy, as the amount of oil in floating storage has fallen in recent weeks. It is unclear whether these market players continue to dance with the contango or are merely finding another home for excess barrels.
Contango refers to a price structure where prices on the spot market offer a discount over futures contracts, leaving profit to be reaped by buying and storing a product, in this case oil. At times of weak freight rates and low oil prices, storing oil on tankers becomes a popular option after onshore storage has been filled, especially if its futures price promises a bonanza. As shown in the chart below, the slope of the curve shows profit potential. The economics supporting crude oil storage on tankers, however, have weakened in recent months as the difference between contracts to buy West Texas Intermediate for prompt and forward delivery has narrowed.

A number of factors conspired to make storage beneficial for both charterers and owners this year. In December of 2008, with oil prices low in the aftermath of economic collapse, storage fixtures started to have a noticeable impact on the market. A flurry of such fixtures in last December and January took ships out of major markets and helped create some additional support for freight rates. Storage fixtures were welcomed by owners as opportunities to keep vessels employed and maintain their oil company approvals, which typically lapse after about six months without carrying oil. While contango has remained in the picture since the March's high, the narrowing spread has left little room for error for traders looking to churn out profit.
There have been a number of signals that traders are reacting to in starting to take the oil stored on tankers ashore. One of the most immediate indicators likely influencing crude storage decisions is on‐shore stocking levels having started to ease back from highs reached earlier in the year. Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) stocks of on‐shore commercial crude oil have fallen by 30 million barrels since March. Storage levels at the Cushing, Oklahoma NYMEX delivery site fell by more than 20 percent between July and September this year. Whether these draw‐downs reflect actual changes in demand or just the perception of changes is not yet clear, but they have been seen as influencing traders.
Many market players invest in oil futures in tandem with currency investment strategies and the declining value of the US dollar is thought to have also been a major force helping narrow the crude oil contango. Production cuts from the Organization for Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) have also played a role, limiting supply and driving up prices for certain crude oils on the spot market.

Last month, retreating sea ice allowed two multipurpose heavy‐lift project carriers to complete a voyage through the Northeast Passage from South Korea, around the Russian Arctic, and on to Rotterdam. Beluga Shipping, the German company whose vessels completed the trip, called it the first non‐Russian commercial voyage through the route. Upon the trip's completion, some commentators heralded the opened sea lane as a global warming's "silver lining." While news of the recent transit is newsworthy, claims that the Northeast Passage will transform trade routes in the near term are overblown. Complexities associated with Arctic navigation, including hull‐type and draft restrictions, added costs and unpredictability are likely to limit use of the route for the foreseeable future. Over the long term, however, the opening of the Northeast Passage may help shape future trade flows. As far as tankers are concerned, the location of oil is the key element.
The ice‐classed 12,744 dwt Beluga Fraternity and Beluga Foresight were carrying power plant equipment when they departed from Ulsan, South Korea in late July. After entering the passage's eastern end near Vladivostok, Russia on August 21, the vessels were escorted by Russian nuclear‐powered icebreakers through the Vilkizki Strait, considered the most treacherous leg of the journey.

The traditional route takes ships through the South China Sea, past Singapore, around India and through the Suez Canal.
Earlier this summer, Norway's foreign minister told an audience in England that the "pirate‐free" route would cut tanker transit times between Europe and Asia by 40 percent within a decade, fueling speculation that the Northeast Passage could emerge as a summertime competitor to the Suez Canal. The fundamental forces that shape tanker trade flows, however, do not currently support a significant role for this newly‐traversable route. Very little oil moves from Japan to Europe, and exports of North Sea oil have been on the decline for many years. Also, the Northeast Passage offers no logistical benefit for tankers loading in Saudi Arabia and other key oil producing areas such as countries in West Africa.
Shorter transit time and reduced fuel consumption would certainly offer some savings for shippers of finished goods using the Northeast Passage alternative, but there are a number of extra costs likely to accompany the voyage which might eliminate the promised savings. Vessels do need to be ice class in order to use the Northeast Passage, adding an estimated 20 percent to the cost of any newbuilding vessel. Absent a dramatic increase in the speed of the ice's recession, even ice class vessels transiting the Passage route will need to be escorted by ice‐breaking vessels. The charges for these services are likely to be subject to vessel availability, threatening further delays that could use money saved by using the shorter route.
The need for ice breaker accompaniment also underscores the difficulty of navigating through the Northeast Passage, another factor likely to limit its attractiveness to tankers looking to travel from Asia to Europe. Even when the ice has retreated enough to make transiting the Passage possible, significant quantities of sea ice remain to pose ever‐present threats. The depth of the Northeast Passage has been estimated at 15 meters, limiting the size of ships that could potentially use the route and further complicating hopes of a summertime sea highway at the top of the world.
Ice delays, unforeseen territorial and diplomatic hurdles as well as having to wait for the formulation of a convoy for an ice breaker to escort would all complicate efforts to plan an efficient shipping schedule. Without the ability for such planning, no significant traffic volumes will likely make their way to the Northeast Passage in the near future. An additional layer of uncertainty is added when considering the shaky understanding of the scientific forces behind climate change.

The rapid growth of China's oil demand has forced a transition from self‐sufficiency enjoyed in the early 1990s toward dependence on imports for about half of its crude oil requirement. Managing their growing import dependence has become a central concern of policy planners in Beijing and an important factor in the development of present and future tanker trade routes.
As shown in the chart below, Chinese crude oil production has remained flat in recent years as its demand has risen sharply. Offshore developments are in the near future, but have yet to come to market. The IEA expects China to experience 5.1 percent (410 kbd) oil demand growth in 2009 and a further 4.1 percent growth (340 kbd) in 2010.

A $586 billion stimulus package China launched last year to counteract the impact of the economic crisis was focused on boosting domestic consumption of goods and services. The National Development and Reform Commission of China recently released statistics reporting that the economy grew at an 8.9 percent annualized rate in the third quarter of 2009.
China's economic development has been a clear factor determining future oil demand for some time, but recent upstream acquisitions have demonstrated the country's interest in taking the reins on security of supply. China has capitalized on asset prices partially deflated by the economic crisis to acquire stakes in a wide variety of oil and gas projects; estimates of the total spent on energy related mergers and acquisition this year vary around $15 billion. China has also entered into about $50 billion of loan‐for‐oil agreements with many producers since 2008. With a dearth of liquidity in the market, it seems more international eyes are turning east.

As the Halloween holiday comes creeping in, many shipowners find themselves wondering if the next few weeks will bring a trick or a treat from the markets. The economy in the United States seemed to have received a treat earlier this week when the Department of Commerce reported 3.5 percent economic growth during the third quarter of this year. The GDP growth beat economists' expectations and fueled a spike in crude oil and other commodity prices. The first signs of growth in over a year also inspired speculation that the economic recovery is moving into its next phase. Spot market VLCC availabilities in the Arabian Gulf have been on the decline, which has undoubtedly helped to secure stronger earnings for owners, especially those with vessels heading east. Down significantly from early 2009 highs, current availabilities of VLCCs 30 days out point to less of a supply overhang, providing owners with vessels in the region more leverage.
The reduction and eventual flattening of recent VLCC availabilities has caused earnings on two benchmark VLCC voyages from the Arabian Gulf to rise simultaneously, as shown in the chart below. Earnings on those two voyages have improved since the second week in October, with the more active Arabian Gulf - Far East route displaying a $10,000 improvement to $27,500 per day.

Each year, the Worldscale Association adjusts the flat rates which serve as the starting point for negotiating the cost of carrying crude oil and refined products on tankers. Under normal conditions, this annual revision ritual does not have a dramatic impact on tanker markets, aside from forcing owners and charterers to adjust to the new rates during the first weeks of the year. Following five straight years of flat rate increases, Worldscale's downward revision of its 2010 flat rates, announced yesterday, reverses some 2009's usual characteristics rates and sets the stage for another round of negotiation between owners and charterers at year's end.
After a 38% average rise in flat rates in 2009, the decrease among the 111 rate revisions announced by Worldscale yesterday averaged 22%. As shown in the chart below, the 2010 flat rate decrease marks an end to recent flat rate increases on key tanker voyages. In general, the rates for longer routes recorded bigger drops, but the impact of these changes will vary from market to market.

Changing trade and consumption patterns, ever‐tightening environmental regulation and the pace of global economic recovery must all be considered alongside the other fundamentals long assumed to propel crude oil and tanker markets. Tanker Prospects, soon to be published by Poten & Partners for the 13 th consecutive year, includes such analysis and can be a valuable tool in commercial strategy development.
The past year has seen rapidly contracting demand for crude oil and refined products impact spot tanker markets while the credit crunch not only limited sale and purchase activity, but also strained those invested in the looming orderbook. As shown in the chart below, 2009 spot market earnings failed to reach the levels set in recent years and marked the end of one of the strongest earnings periods in the history of the tanker market. There have been encouraging signs regarding oil demand and the wider economy of late, but few would doubt that it has been a very challenging past year for the tanker market and considerable uncertainty remains about its future.

Foremost among the uncertainties currently facing the tanker market is the pace of orderbook deliveries. As in past downturns, the delivery of vessels ordered at the height of the market continues to hold down freight rates still struggling to recover. Shipowners and shipyards are currently negotiating delays and deferments, but the timing of these deliveries is subject to many influences. It remains to be seen how the market will absorb this tonnage.
While delivery of the orderbook will be the key metric over the medium term, the near‐term prospects for the tanker industry remain tied to recovery in the international economy. China's infrastructure spending and Saudi Arabian power generation were cited as the main drivers for the International Energy Agency's (IEA) 220 kbd upward revision of its 2009 oil demand projection released yesterday. IEA also reported evidence of stronger‐than‐expected fuel consumption in the US and in October the Department of Commerce reported that the American economy grew at a 3.5 percent annualized rate in the third quarter of 2009. While modest, the fourth quarter demand growth expected by the IEA would mark the first year‐on‐year quarterly increase since the second quarter of 2008 as well as a milestone on the long road to recovery.
The central role of developing nations in shaping near term expectations for growth should come as no surprise. It has been widely acknowledged that the emerging nations of the East, especially China and India, will be the likely sources for the majority of crude oil and refined product demand growth in the coming years. Less often acknowledged is the fact that expanding oil demand in these markets will translate into increased ton‐mile demand in unpredictable ways. In order to benefit from opportunities in those markets it is necessary to first build a clear understanding of these countries' current role in the petroleum industry and expectations of how those roles transform global tanker trade routes.

Late last month, a malfunctioning valve on the barge supplying a product tanker reportedly caused it to spill between 400 and 800 gallons (between 9 and 19 barrels) of bunker fuel into San Francisco Bay. The spill reignited an environmental group's campaign for a ban on the use of residual bunker fuel, an effort initiated following the Cosco Busan spill in 2007. The campaign aims to introduce regulation that would stop the use of the residual bunker fuel in commercial shipping altogether. While tankers have perhaps carried the bulk of the public scrutiny with respect to oil spills, in reality, the statistics speak to the tanker industry's long‐term reduction in the frequency and severity of oil spills.
Tightening of maritime regulation related to fuel spills often follows high‐profile incidents of pollution, and managing public perception can be a very important part of maintaining a workable regulatory regime. The influence of the Exxon Valdez on the public's perception of the risk of oil spills from tankers continues to loom large 20 years after the incident, despite the fact that it ranks as only the 35 th largest spill recorded. The public perception and media coverage reiterate the need for the tanker industry to raise awareness of the safety and prevention measures in place and its improved record in the context of growing volumes transported by sea.
According to the International Tanker Owners Pollution Federation (ITOPF), oil spills from tankers reached their lowest level on record last year, even though ocean transportation of oil expands every year. This represents the continuation of a long‐term trend over the past decade towards fewer significant pollution incidents from tankers. Defined as a spill over 700 tons (approximately 5,000 barrels), the number of significant spills involving tankers, according to the ITOPF, has fallen from 34 in 1979 to just one in 2008. As shown in the chart below, these significant spills have also constituted an increasingly smaller portion of total spills since 1970s.

The ITOPF has tracked accidental spills by tankers, combined carriers and barges since 1974. The group categorizes small spills as those involving less than 7 tons, medium‐sized spills as between 7 and 700 tons and large spills (as mentioned) as anything exceeding 700 tons. ITOPF research is aimed at identifying areas in which spills are occurring and working with local partners to strengthen preparedness. In recent years, for example, the organization has taken steps to improve its cooperation with partners in China, where it reports an increasing incidence of tanker spills.
Publicity garnered by a particular oil spill can often determine whether it leads to increased regulation. According to the ITOPF, the total amount of oil spilled from tankers in recorded incidents during 2008 was 2,000 tons, a significant drop from the 330,000 tons recorded in 1970. This decrease is all the more noteworthy when considered in light of the significant increase in the volume of oil moving on tankers that has occurred since the 1970s.

Well‐intentioned as it may be, there are several problems with responding to the recent spill with a ban on the use of residual bunker fuel. Primarily, this initiative ignores the ongoing tightening of marine fuel regulation which is already underway. The International Maritime Organization adopted regulations last October calling for significant reductions in the sulfur content of marine bunker fuel over the next ten years and has also set new nitrogen oxide (NOx) limits for marine diesel engines installed on newly‐built vessels. In addition, fuel quality legislation from the European Union as well as more stringent regulation from California have all been introduced in recent years to address harmful emissions from ships. While these regulations target emissions rather than spills, they do have an enormous potential impact and must be considered as part of the context of the wider energy and shipping markets the proposed ban looks to influence.
A fierce debate is already underway about the sustainability of these regulations and any effort to speed the phase‐out of residual bunker fuel further seems likely to encounter stiff resistance. Finally, at a time when fuel costs are once again rising sufficiently to threaten recovery in the tanker market, the added costs that would accompany a wholesale switch to marine distillate must be considered carefully.
The recent San Francisco spill is regrettable, but does not present an urgent need to tighten regulation on the use of residual bunker fuel. For the tanker industry, the spill serves as its own reminder of the importance of continuing efforts to improve practices. As demonstrated by the ITOPF's statistics, the amount of oil spilled from tankers has decreased over time. Owing partially to the work of organizations like the International Tanker Owners Pollution Federation, there is reason to believe tankers can lead the way as those improvements continue.

For many in the tanker industry, 2009 has been a tough year. Shipowners and charterers alike can commiserate about low demand for crude oil and refined products as well as the limping pace of growth in many economies. That said, the Thanksgiving holiday seems to spark some excitement that the market could be poised for a turnaround ‐ if only based on past years' experience! The 2007 Thanksgiving holiday began one of the most extraordinary rallies in the history of the tanker market. Spot VLCC rates jumped by 50 points overnight and kicked off a 12 month period of unusually strong earnings for shipowners. This time last year, with the burgeoning economic crisis dominating the headlines, tanker markets were fighting off some negativity and still performing despite the gloomy broader sentiment. Since there is some strengthening in the spot tanker market at present, is another spike just a few days away?
Seasons Come...
In addition to heightened seasonal demand for crude oil, November often brings weather conditions, such as increased fog and tropical storms, which cause delays and lead to ships out of position. These drivers give additional support, if only temporary, to freight rates.
The most basic variable which can increase volatility in rates is related to oil demand and it is most easily represented through changes in the number of tanker liftings. There has been an average of 64 percent difference between monthly highs and lows in the number of liftings from the Arabian Gulf between 1995 and 2008. As shown in the chart below, the number of spot liftings from the Arabian Gulf has demonstrated less volatility this year and remained below monthly averages throughout 2009. In periods of heightened demand, month‐on‐month availability of ships can make the difference between an average and extraordinary market.

While the extreme volatility that drove the market to new highs in late 2007 and early 2008 has receded, participants in the tanker industry should continue expecting the unexpected.

US refiners are being forced to deal with dismal margins brought about by a lack of demand for their prime products - gasoline and diesel. Consumption of gasoline is roughly 7 percent less than the go‐go days of mid‐2007 - and once the growth in ethanol use is considered, the need for refiners' hydrocarbon component has contracted even more. Diesel use has evaporated by some one million barrels per day (mbd) or over 20 percent from its highs of late 2007.
Margins have suffered from the collision between fairly strong crude oil prices and refiners' lack of leverage to raise product prices in the face of weak demand. But after living in a cyclic industry for many years, most refiners are adept at dealing with business pull‐backs. Past recessions have generally seen some refining capacity close while other capacity is either expanded or added. In keeping with the law‐of‐the‐jungle, economically strong refineries become stronger while weak ones get closed and, of course, life goes on. But this recession somehow seems different. With green house gas (GHG) cap and trade regulations - as well as the associated costs - still being forged on the anvil of political wrangling, strong US refiners may pause before rushing to offset any closed capacity.

The seemingly endless line of storm clouds gathering around US refiners does not appear to bode well for people trying to make a living carrying crude oil to the shores of this nation. While domestic refining capacity in a few niche markets may weather the pending GHG allocation storm, some of those located in markets with easy access to imports may become pressured financially and eventually succumb. Conventional reasoning might see shrinking US refining capacity yielding expectations of greater product imports. But if the mandated leap in biofuels production does indeed come to pass, any growth in imports may be muted. Ship owners will likely call on their agility to balance their fleets against shifting US demand for both dirty and clean tonnage.
Surviving a paralyzing or lethal blow - commonly referred to as a whammy - is usually a mixture of planning, skill and just plain luck. Make no mistake though: the coming US GHG regulations represent a whammy that will propel the concept of conducting business‐as‐usual into antiquity. Only through intense planning, skill and a perhaps a dose of luck will agile and adaptive businesses survive in the future's GHG emission constricted paradigm. Here's to hoping Washington realizes the long‐term impacts of regulations on American business before it's too late.

In the weeks and months leading up to the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) in Copenhagen, expectations ran high that the meeting would produce a concrete emissions‐reduction framework to replace that of the Kyoto Protocol. As the discussions progress, it becomes more apparent that a resolution may not be forthcoming. With the first of two weeks of the IPCC coming to an end, the consensus on climate change is now under siege and hopes for the current session have been scaled back to yielding just a political basis for future negotiations (mind your pockets, taxpayers). The divide between developed and developing countries has emerged as a dominant theme: while the two groups generally agree on the need for a massive reduction in worldwide carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions, the impasse has not surprisingly been on the most critical question; who will pay for it?
The International Energy Agency estimates that capping CO2 emissions at target levels could cost more than $10 trillion between 2010 and 2030. The first week of debate at the UN conference has focused on distributing these costs between industrialized countries responsible for past emissions and the developing nations which are the likely source for the majority of future emissions growth. Each of the more than 190 nations attending the conference in Denmark has brought their own perspective to the issue, but thus far the most prominent division has been between China and the United States. As shown in the chart below, China and the United States account for more than 40 percent of global CO2 emissions, making their cooperation on the matter critical to success.

text: President Obama hopes Copenhagen will produce a new framework that includes legally binding emissions‐reduction targets for developing countries, especially China and India. It was the lack of such binding targets for developing countries which prevented Congressional approval of the 1997 Kyoto Protocol. The effort to coax these commitments from the world's emerging economies has been complicated by the uncertainty surrounding current U.S. energy policy. Legislation that narrowly passed the House of Representatives in June would commit the United States to a cap and trade system aiming to bring about a 17 percent reduction from 2005 emission levels by 2020. A companion bill currently stalled in the Senate increases the emissions reduction target to 20 percent in the same time period, but the 17 percent reduction approved by the House (equivalent to a three percent reduction from 1990 levels) constituted the Obama Administration's opening position at the Copenhagen talks. Whether it will hurt the United States' economy (or any other economy) in the process seems to have escaped the attention of decision makers.

China has tried to change the metric for measuring progress on emissions reduction from total emissions to one of emissions intensity. The concept of carbon intensity measures emissions per unit of GDP and allows China to highlight that while it is the world's largest greenhouse gas emitter by volume, it has much lower per capita emissions than the United States and other industrialized countries. In November, China announced its intension to lower the emissions‐ intensity of its economy by between 40 and 45 percent by 2020 to balance environmental concerns with the need for economic growth.
The carbon intensity metric has made China the natural voice of a group of countries, including India, South Africa and others that are logically concerned that ad hoc regulation of carbon emissions would constrain their development. These countries have called for their industrialized counterparts to commit to a 40 percent emissions reduction from 1990 levels by 2020 and create a mechanism for funding clean energy technology in developing nations. When the Copenhagen conference began, industrialized countries responded by endorsing a proposal for a $10 billion per year fund to be transferred to developing countries to help them with the potential impact of climate change. In the opening days of the conference, the White House said a consensus was forming around the idea, which it said would form a core element of any agreement produced in Copenhagen. Such a fund would also buy world leaders two years of negotiating time before the Kyoto Protocol formally expires in 2012. US officials have pledged to pay into any such fund, but Todd Stern, the Obama Administration's chief negotiator at the talks, rejected the idea of "reparations" by developed countries to make up for decades of emissions. Stern said the $10 billion fund would focus on the poorest countries and made especially clear he did not expect the fund to compensate China for its emissions cuts. Where does this funding stop? How are funds allocated, overseen and administered? The leaders seem to be neglecting these hugely important details.
At a time when industrialized countries are still recovering from the economic crisis, it is unrealistic to expect them to pay for the developing world's transition to a cleaner economy as they attempt similar transitions themselves.
The fact that China does not fit comfortably into either the "developing" or "developed" country labels has been the source of much of the friction on display over the past week in Denmark. Beijing's efforts to lead developing nations and shift the focus from total emissions to emissions intensity may win ideological support, but does not change the underlying realities. Slower growth of emissions is not less emissions and focusing on carbon intensity may ultimately slow progress towards real economic growth.
With China's surging demand expected to be the source of about half of carbon emissions growth in coming decades, any effective international climate change agreement needs Chinese support. Two points highlight the lack of faith in the development of a meaningful framework: the inability of signers and supporters of Kyoto to actually meet the first set of emissions targets and the innate interest of many world leaders boondoggle again in Copenhagen.

In a press release for its Annual Energy Outlook, the Energy Information Administration (EIA) candidly acknowledges that the United States is unlikely to meet long‐term biofuels blending targets. Significant doubts also remain as to whether or not the United States will even be able to produce the level of biofuels mandated for blending next year. Moreover, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is taking extra time to consider raising the allowable ethanol gasoline blending percentage from the current limit of 10 to 15 percent. Also, a recent report from the Government Accountability Office (GAO) explores biofuels' detrimental impact on water supplies. Finally, it seems that a long‐overdue reevaluation of the nation's biofuels policy is underway.
The Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) was created by the Energy Policy Act of 2005 and called for increasing inclusion of biofuels in the nation's fuel supply. Under the system, individual producers, importers and blenders were given yearly biofuels blending quotas. The 2007 Energy Independence and Security Act (EISA) extended the RFS and broadened it to include other forms of biofuels, calling for 11.1 billion gallons to be blended into the fuel supply in 2009, with the amount rising incrementally towards 36 billion gallons in 2022.

This past March, an application for a waiver to raise the maximum allowable ethanol content in gasoline from 10 to 15 percent was submitted by a coalition of ethanol producers. The coalition's proposal was an effort to help their struggling industry, which is threatened by dropping gasoline demand and the auto parc's move towards more efficient vehicles.
At the beginning of December, the EPA announced it would delay a decision on the waiver until mid 2010, but indicated that it was indeed considering raising the allowable blending level. EPA said that two tests had shown that engines in cars built after 2001 can likely handle blends higher than 10 percent. The EPA still needs more vehicles to be tested before approving the waiver and expects testing to be completed by May.
The Clean Air Act prohibits the EPA from introducing any new gasoline additive before proving that it does not "cause or contribute" to engine failure. Ethanol blending up to 10 percent is sanctioned under a 1978 waiver. Opposition to the recent ethanol waiver proposal has focused on the possibility of damage to engines not designed for higher ethanol blends. The Alliance of Automobile Manufactures praised the EPA's postponement of its decision and said that all steps should be taken to ensure that higher level blends do not damage vehicles' engines, fuel lines or emissions systems before any waiver is approved. The American Petroleum Institute also lauded EPA's delay of the decision, but raised concerns about the possibility of granting a waiver that would accommodate only part of the vehicle fleet. The National Petrochemical & Refiners Association questioned the data supporting the waiver request and said that at least two years of study would be required in order to prove such "mid‐level" blends are safe for engines and the environment. An executive from the Outdoor Power Equipment Institute told reporters that higher ethanol blends could cause leaks and fires in portable equipment.

One of the reasons the EIA expects the US to fall short of the goals set forth in the original RFS is that they were formulated on assumptions of continued technological progress in the development of non‐grain, "second generation" cellulosic biofuels. Cellulosic biofuels are those derived from renewable biomass feedstocks such as fast growing grasses, cereal straw and forest residues among others. The 2007 EISA stipulated that 21 of 36 billion gallons of biofuels used to meet the RFS in 2022 should come from such advanced biofuels and the government has provided grants to support research and development of such biofuels.
But beyond the present challenging economic environment they share with first generation biofuels, significant technical challenges remain to widespread introduction of advanced biofuels. A widely‐quoted estimate predicts production of cellulosic biofuels in the United States will remain under 40 million gallons in 2010.

During his campaign, President Obama called for higher volumes of advanced biofuels partially to ensure the overall sustainability of the biofuels program. Now it appears that the program is coming under greater scrutiny. The Government Accountability Office recently released a report on the effect of increased levels of biofuels production on national water supplies. The report explained that biofuels' impact on water supplies vary widely by feedstock and are distinct for the cultivating and subsequent processing of each feedstock. The GAO reported that growing corn for ethanol, which requires heavy use of irrigated water, is more water intensive than other biofuel feedstocks and could result increased water pollution from fertilizers. The report also echoed experts' concerns about the ethanol's corrosive properties and resulting problems with storage. Threats to drinking water and aquatic life from the emission of chemicals and salts from ethanol refineries were also examined.
While the GAO listed technological fixes for the problems with water supply ‐ including conservation- these fixes were noted as being far from cost‐effective. The report also said it was premature to know the water impact of second generation biofuels yet to be commercialized on a large scale and urged consideration of the regional variability in water resources within the United States when formulating investment decisions or support for biofuels.
